pages.text:
*From the Dropout Club Handbook, Rule 6: Meetings begin with biscuits.*

The sun was just a thin pink line on the horizon when Marnie Pennywhistle tiptoed out of the broom shop. Her basket clinked with eight jam sandwiches, heavy as bricks. One spare broom leaned against her hip, bristles stiff. A note in Gran’s shaky script said, *Good luck with whatever this is.* Marnie tucked it into her cardigan pocket, next to her heart, which felt slightly too large for a Tuesday morning.

The Potting Shed waited in the dark, smelling of wet earth and old roses. Dew beaded on the clay pots, catching the first light. And there, standing outside in the grey shadows, was Bunt. He was holding a kettle the size of a small cauldron, his barrel-boots silent on the grass. He did not sneeze. He had not cast a spell. He was just standing there, which, for Bunt, was the most magical thing of all.

“Morning,” Bunt rumbled, his voice like a cello string being plucked gently. “I brought tea. And biscuits. And a mild suspicion that we are about to do something very silly.”

Marnie looked at the kettle, then at the troll, then at the sky, which was turning from grey to a hopeful, bruised purple.

“Silly is better than sad,” she said, and unlocked the door.
pages.image: A grey-green troll with moss hair and barrel boots holds a large silver kettle in the pre-dawn mist of a garden shed, while a girl with copper-red buns and a yellow cardigan peers at him from the doorway, holding a wicker basket.

pages.text:
Toby pointed at a rickety wooden bench. “Demolish,” he said, in his precise, clipped voice.

The bench groaned, stretched, and popped itself together into a cozy sofa with a tufted back. Marnie blinked. Toby shrugged. “It works backwards, but it works.”

Marnie pointed at the dust bunnies under the stove. “Tidy,” she whispered.

Poof. Three real bunnies sat on the floor, looking deeply confused. One, a grey one with a smudge of soot on its nose, stayed. “Dust Bunny,” named Lulu, before apologizing to the rabbit for naming it.

Lulu, feeling generous, pointed at the window. “Please clean,” she said.

One hundred and four lavender-scented socks appeared in a heap. They stretched and draped themselves into curtains, cushions, a rug, and a hammock that sagged precariously over the stove.

“It’s functional,” Toby said, adjusting his glasses.

“It’s a disaster,” said Marnie.

“It’s home,” said Bunt, taking a biscuit from the sock-cushion.
pages.image: A cozy, chaotic garden shed interior with a sofa made of wood, a hammock of mismatched lavender socks, and three small rabbits sitting near a pot-bellied stove while a girl, a boy in a navy vest, and a troll look on.

pages.text:
Marnie hauled out a thick slab of chalk. It looked like a single white toothpick in Bunt's massive, grey-green hand. Toby held the board steady.

Rule 1 was already on the door in Marnie's wobbly chalk, so Toby copied it into the Handbook in neat, slanted letters, and went on without being asked. “Rule 2: Gran is always right, especially when she is wrong.”

“She will be thrilled,” said Marnie.

Lulu raised a hand. “I’m sorry, but I think we need a rule about socks. Socks are not a spell. Socks are a lifestyle.” She apologized to the board for suggesting it.

Toby scribbled. “Rule 3: If a spell goes the wrong way, check which way you were facing.” He looked very pleased with himself. Lulu’s rule became Rule 4. Bunt cleared his throat and added, in his slow voice, “Rule 5: When in doubt, stand upwind of the troll.”

Gerald, the goose, waddled over. He snatched the chalk from Bunt's fingers, held it in his orange beak, and honked loudly. The sound was sharp and demanding.

Bunt blinked his slow, mossy eyes. “He wants a biscuit.”

Marnie traded a chocolate digestive for the chalk. When Gerald finally dropped it, she wrote the last rule of the morning: “Rule 6: Meetings begin with biscuits.” They elected Gerald Honorary Chair, because he cannot be argued with, being a goose.

Toby nodded solemnly, adjusting his glasses. “A fair legal precedent.”
pages.image: Gerald with a purple starred ribbon stands on a table holding a piece of chalk in its beak, looking imperious, while a troll offers a biscuit and a girl with freckles writes on a blackboard behind them.

pages.text:
The first official meeting began with a question hanging in the air. It smelled faintly of lavender and damp wool.

“If your magic ever worked correctly,” Toby said, tapping the board with his finger, “what would you do?”

Lulu raised her striped sock. It looked lonely. “A pair. Just one perfect pair. No more heaping. I could wear them without explaining to everyone why I have fourteen toes.”

Bunt cleared his throat. The sound was like a large rock rolling down a gravel driveway. “Stand in a classroom. Not sneeze. For ten minutes. That would be a personal victory.”

Marnie looked at her hands. They were still dusty from the chalk. She did not want a pair of socks, and she certainly did not want a quiet classroom. She wanted to cast one correct spell, just once, so that nobody could ever say she couldn’t. She wanted the fish to be a candle, the moustache to stay down, and the goose to be a hat.

Nobody said she shouldn’t want it. That was the most surprising part of the morning. Toby simply added it to the list. His pen scratched softly against the wood.

“One correct spell,” he said, nodding to himself. “Goal achieved. Biscuits all round.”

Marnie felt a small, warm weight settle in her chest.
pages.image: Four characters sit around a table in a shed, listening to a boy in glasses speak, while Gerald looks on from a chair; the mood is supportive and quiet, with soft light from a window.

pages.text:
Evening fell, and with it, a strange, glittering mist drifted down the hill from the Academy.

Bunt sniffed the air. His nose twitched. “Ah... ah... AH-CHOO!”

A wave of pure, quiet force blew across the garden. It pushed the dust, the socks, and the fear all the way to the far side of the shed. In the silence that followed, the world felt very still.

Far above, on the hill, a golden light bloomed. It was the Golden Circle, rehearsing. The light was so bright and perfect it made every shadow in the garden stand up straight and point at the sky. The flowers stopped swaying. The wind held its breath.

Marnie felt a chill, not of cold, but of wrongness. She looked at the perfect light, then at the messy, sock-filled shed, and for the first time, she was glad to be on the side that was a little bit crooked.
pages.image: A hilltop school glowing with intense golden light against a dark blue evening sky, casting long, straight, rigid shadows down a grassy hill towards a small, crooked shed with Gerald looking up.
